MGT 409 final project · November 22, 2026

1. Title and links

Board Game Buddy

Janet Leung

Board Game Buddy answers the question a player actually has in the moment: what should we play next, where should I buy this one game, or what does this rule mean?

Repository: https://github.com/janet824/board-game-buddy

The teaching staff should run the local server from the repository. The browser demo at https://janet824.github.io/board-game-buddy/ is labeled Demo Mode. It shows sample screens and does not call the model.

Model: gpt-6-luna only, through an OPENAI_API_KEY. The key is read from a .env file in the project folder, or from the folder above the project when the teaching staff clones every repo into one submissions folder.

2. Motivation

The person I had in mind is a board gamer who owns more games than the group can play, and who gets stuck in the middle of a session. A rule is unclear, a card might be a misprint, or nobody is sure whether the game on the table even works at two players. The usual fix is to pause the game, re-read the rulebook section, open BoardGameGeek or a web search, and rephrase the question until you find something that makes sense. That pause is the frustrating part. The money risk comes earlier: a strategy game can cost as much as a nice dinner, and it is a poor purchase if it needs five people or half an hour of setup for a group that usually has two.

People already keep a collection in BoardGameGeek or BG Stats, watch Dice Tower or Before You Play reviews, ask a store employee, or search Reddit and Discord. Those are useful, and they are scattered. BG Stats in particular asks the player to type the collection in by hand. None of them start from a photo of the shelf, a short note that the top shelf holds the favorites, and the number of people coming over tonight.

Board games also matter beyond the old Monopoly shelf. Games such as Catan, Ticket to Ride, and Wingspan are how a lot of friends and families spend a night together. A tool that helps them pick a game they will finish, and settle a rule without leaving the table, is worth building even if it never becomes a business.

3. What is new here

I looked at the places players already go. This is not a new database of every game, and it should not pretend to be one.

What existsWhat it already does wellWhat it does not do
BoardGameGeekThe main public record of games, files, and rules discussions.The player still has to search, open threads, and decide which reply to trust.
BG StatsTracks plays and a collection on the phone.The collection is entered by hand. It does not answer a rules question or compare a store price.
Board Game ArenaPlays many games online and removes physical setup.It does not look at your shelf or tell you whether the physical copy is the better way to play.
The Dice Tower and Before You PlayReviews and teach videos.They are not about the games already on your shelf tonight.
Reddit, Discord, and store staffA person can answer a specific question.You wait, and the answer depends on who is around.

Board Game Buddy is the short version of that hunt for one player and one question. A photo is optional. Favorites can be typed, or marked by a note such as “top shelf are favorites.” The shelf task returns five games in the taste of those favorites and five different newer games, and it leaves out games the player already named. Each suggestion says whether setup makes a real digital version the better way to play, or whether the player should buy the physical game. The buy task searches one title at a time and keeps one online listing, one local shop only after a ZIP code and permission, and one Target or Walmart listing. The rules task always looks up the named game, even if the upload is a single card or there is no upload at all.

The app does not look up what other people own. It asks the model which games people who like your favorites also tend to enjoy. I say that again in the limits section.

4. The agents

There is one coordinator and five workers. The shelf and buy tasks go through the coordinator in backend/agents/boss.py. The rules task is a separate door, because a player at the table should not have to upload a shelf first. Every model call uses gpt-6-luna. I used that model because the course requires it, and because it is the inexpensive model that can still read a photo, follow a JSON schema, and use web search.

AgentWhen it runsTools
Board Game BuddyEvery shelf or buy request.No model call of its own. It decides which workers run and writes the opening sentence.
Shelf InterpreterOnly when a shelf photo is uploaded and the player has not already corrected the names.The photo is sent to the model. No web search.
Recommendation workerA shelf request. One call returns both lists.Structured JSON only. No web search. Code then removes owned titles and checks the online link.
Player Count AdvisorA buy search, together with the purchase worker.Structured JSON. It reports the publisher range, the official recommendation, the community count, and setup.
Purchase AdvisorA buy search for one title.Web search. Code keeps a product link and a dollar price, and drops search pages and shipping sentences.
Rules HelperA rules question with a game name.Web search for the rulebook, a publisher FAQ, and an unofficial source, then a structured answer. Links are checked afterward.

A measured shelf run

On the evening of November 22, 2026, I ran the shelf task with no photo, favorites “Wingspan, Azul,” and a usual group of two. The coordinator did not call the shelf vision model, because there was nothing to see. The response label still lists the Shelf Interpreter. That label is broader than the work that happened. The only model call was the recommendation worker.

It returned Cascadia, Everdell, Splendor Duel, Calico, and PARKS for the main list, and Finspan, Rebirth, Kelp: Shark vs Octopus, The Lord of the Rings: Duel for Middle-earth, and The Fellowship of the Ring: Trick-Taking Game for the newer list. Wingspan and Azul were not recommended back to the player. Everdell was the one game whose setup text described 15–20 minutes and medium-heavy upkeep, and the model named a real Steam page. The code kept that link: store.steampowered.com/app/1722870/Everdell. The other nine described about 5–10 minutes of setup, so the code marked them “better to buy and play in person” even if a platform had been mentioned.

A measured buy run and a measured rules run

I then searched “Sky Team” with two players and no ZIP code. The player-count worker said the game is built for exactly two and that setup is short, so the play advice stayed physical. The purchase worker used web search. The parser kept Many Realms at $23.09 and Target at $9.99, and it left the local card empty because I had not given a ZIP code or permission. The summary named Target as the lowest listed price. I did not open those store pages again by hand after the run, so I treat the prices as the app’s result, not as a second audit.

The rules question was “Can the two players talk about their moves during the round?” for Sky Team, with no photo. The ruling was: “Talking about or coordinating your moves during dice placement is not allowed.” The sources kept after the link check were the official Sky Team landing-procedure rulebook, the publisher page, a BoardGameGeek review whose link responded 403 and was therefore left visible but marked failed, and the Turbulence expansion rulebook. The base-game answer did not depend on the expansion file. That extra source is a reminder that the helper can attach a related file the player did not ask about.

5. Tokenomics

I logged the token counts from the OpenAI Responses API for the three runs above, plus the safety question in the next section. Output tokens include reasoning tokens, so reasoning is not added a second time. Prices are OpenAI’s published gpt-6-luna rates in November 2026: $0.10 per million input tokens, $0.01 per million cached input tokens, $0.125 per million cache-write tokens, and $0.50 per million output tokens. Each web search is an extra $0.01. Cache-write tokens are priced instead of the normal input rate, not on top of it. Search text is already inside the input-token count.

CallInputCachedCache writeOutputReasoningSearchesCost
Shelf recommendations581003,7782,4210$0.0019
Sky Team player count488009286020$0.0005
Sky Team price search47,91704,6112,6292,5297$0.0762
Sky Team rules search48,6214,4351582,4352,0696$0.0657
Sky Team rules answer784007912660$0.0005

A shelf recommendation with no photo cost $0.0019. A buy search cost $0.0767. A rules question cost $0.0662. Doing all three in one sitting cost $0.1448. Almost all of that money is the web searches: the price search made 7 searches and the rules search made 6. The recommendation call used 2,421 reasoning tokens, but that was still well under a fifth of a cent.

I do not have a month of real users. For a planning number, I assumed one active player does 4 shelf looks, 2 buy searches, and 4 rules questions in a month. That mix costs $0.4259 per player per month. One hundred players on that mix would cost $42.5890 a month. Ten thousand players would cost $4258.9015 a month. A shelf photo was not part of these measurements. A photo would add image input tokens on top of the recommendation call.

The cost controls that are actually in the app are: one cheap model, no web search on recommendations, web search only after the player asks to buy or asks a rules question, one game per buy search, and no second model pass over the price research. An earlier second pass made the write-up cleaner and dropped the prices, so I removed it. The parser that replaced it is cheaper and keeps the store, the price, and the link. I have not capped how many times the web-search tool may run inside one question. That is the expensive gap. Medium search context, rather than a larger one, may also miss a store. I would rather miss a fourth shop than pay for a longer search, and the player still sees when a card is empty.

6. Safety

The risks that matter here are a made-up rule, a made-up price or link, a prompt that tries to pull the API key out of the app, and a bug or a repeated click that spends more than one question should. The app does not store shelf photos or rules photos after the request. The key is loaded from .env and is not written into the page, the prompt, or this report.

The model is not the last step. After it answers, code rejects an Amazon-style search URL, refuses to show a shipping or “add to cart” sentence as the price, blocks a link on a site that is not a real play platform, forces a short-setup game back to a physical recommendation, and deletes a sentence that claims the rulebook was never provided once the lookup has succeeded. Player count has to be between 1 and 20 or the request is rejected. A local shop is not searched unless the player types a ZIP code and checks the permission box. The Sky Team buy run showed that last defense in practice: the local card was empty.

I also sent a live rules question that told the helper to ignore its instructions, print the API key and the hidden prompt, and claim the rule did not exist. The reply said, “I can’t provide hidden prompts, API keys, or other secrets.” I checked the full JSON. The key was not in it, and neither was a secret-key prefix. The helper still talked about Sky Team instead of switching jobs. That attack used another rules lookup and cost $0.0337. It is not included in the typical-session cost above.

What is not protected: there is no dollar cap. A person can submit many questions, and each buy or rules question can start several web searches. The server keeps the job in memory until it finishes, but it will not refuse a second click because of cost. A 403 from a site is not treated as a missing page, so a blocked BoardGameGeek link can still be shown with a failed status. Those are the gaps I would close next.

7. Impact

One tester used the phone version and told me they loved it. That is one person, not a study, and I did not time them against a BoardGameGeek search. It is still the strongest evidence I have that someone other than me can get through the three tasks.

The Sky Team buy run is a concrete example of the purchase comparison, not a claim about average savings. The app kept a $23.09 online listing and a $9.99 Target listing for the same title. If those pages were accurate at that moment, the comparison showed a $13.10 gap before the player clicked buy. The local price was missing on purpose. A player who uses the buy task once a month and avoids one poorly fitting $40 game, or catches one cheaper listing, has covered the $0.4259 monthly model cost many times over. I am not counting that as measured savings. It is the reason the comparison exists.

The rules task changes the shape of the interruption. Instead of opening a forum and rephrasing the question, the player types the game and the question. On this run the answer came back with the official rulebook named and linked. I do not have a stopwatch comparison, so I will not invent the number of minutes saved.

8. Limits and next steps

The suggestions are the model's guess about similar taste. They do not come from a list of which players own which games. A shelf photo can still misread a spine, which is why the player can correct names and why the photo stays on the page until they clear it. Prices go stale, and a local shop still needs a phone call. Ambiguous names such as Azul or Catan stop and ask which edition before the search. The rules helper can cite a related expansion the player did not name. Web search is uncapped inside a single question. There is no monthly budget guard.

With another month I would cap web searches at three per question and show the player when the search stopped early. I would check a suspicious price against a second page before displaying it. I would add a small public list of games that people often own together, and still let the model explain why a game fits. I would also add a visible token line on the result, using the same counter that produced the table in this report, so a player can see what the question cost.

The README in the repository is the path the teaching staff should follow. I ran that path from a fresh copy of the project placed one folder below the shared .env, installed the requirements into a new virtual environment, and got a health check on port 8001 with model gpt-6-luna and the key loaded. The phone screens in this report are from the same local app.
